name: Chin-to-philtrum ratio

lead: The chin-to-philtrum ratio compares how tall the chin is with how long the philtrum, the groove between nose and upper lip, is. Looksmaxxing communities use it as a quick check of lower-face harmony: a short philtrum with a tall chin, or the reverse, is described as throwing the lower third out of balance.

The often-quoted benchmark is about 1:2, philtrum to chin, though sources define the points differently. Surgical literature discusses lower-third proportions more broadly, and forum users use the ratio to discuss genioplasty, lip lifts and jaw surgery.

paras: People photograph or measure the face from front on, mark the base of the nose, the lip line and the bottom of the chin, and compare the upper-lip segment with the chin segment. Forum members then discuss options for changing it: genioplasty to shorten or lengthen the chin, a lip lift to shorten the philtrum, or jaw surgery that changes the upper jaw position.

The ratio is a screening heuristic and is measured differently by different people, so results vary with photo angle and landmarks. Procedures discussed in connection with it are surgeries with their own risks. A surgeon's assessment weighs lip competence, bite and overall profile, not one ratio.

angle.text: People use the ratio to locate where the lower face looks out of proportion and to frame questions for a surgeon about chin height, lip length and jaw position. It is a planning aid for conversations about procedures, not a procedure itself.

lead: The chin-to-philtrum ratio compares the vertical height of the chin with the length of the philtrum, the vertical groove running from the base of the nose to the upper lip.[1] In looksmaxxing communities it is a shorthand for lower-third harmony: people measure it from front-on photographs and use it to decide whether the lower face looks balanced or whether chin height, lip length or jaw position is the thing to change.[2][3][4][5]

The best-known benchmark in forum discussion is about 1:2, philtrum to chin, though members define the landmarks differently and ask what ranges are acceptable and why the ratio matters.[4][5] Threads on the topic often end in surgical planning, with members discussing a genioplasty to shorten or advance the chin, a lip lift to shorten a long philtrum, or upper-jaw surgery that moves the maxilla.[2][3][6][7][8]

Published facial-proportion work does not name a chin-to-philtrum ratio as a standard, but it describes closely related measures. A narrative review of lip aesthetics reports that the lower facial third is divided into segments for upper lip, lower lip and chin, with roughly 30 percent for the upper lip and 70 percent for lip-plus-chin, and notes that chin height can be reduced to help lip competence.[9]

paras: The philtrum is the groove between the nose and upper lip, bordered by two ridges called philtral columns; in humans it has no known function and forms in the embryo where facial processes meet, which is why incomplete fusion can result in cleft lip.[1] The ratio sets the length of this segment against the chin. Definitions differ: some people measure the chin from the lower lip to the bottom of the chin, others from the stomion (the junction of the lips) to menton, so quoted ideals vary with the method.[4][5]

A review of lip aesthetics gives a related set of proportions: the lower facial third divided into upper lip, lower lip and chin; about 30 percent of lower-third height for the upper lip and 70 percent for lower lip plus chin; and a chin that is on average about 70 percent of lower facial height in contemporary ideals, compared with 66 percent in the classical canon.[9] It also gives an upper-to-lower lip height ratio of 1:1.6 for youthful Caucasian faces and states that some studies have not supported golden-ratio models of attractiveness.[9]

Measured values depend on the photo angle, head posture and landmark choice, and on the population studied. A 2019 cross-sectional study using 3D photography of 100 healthy adults aged 20 to 30 from southern Spain with normal occlusion reported sex differences in several lower-face measures: chin height (Li-Me) averaged about 39.1 mm in men and 38.1 mm in women, upper-lip vermilion height was greater in men, and lower-lip height did not differ significantly by sex.[10] The study did not define a philtrum-to-chin ideal.[10]
The review of lip aesthetics adds that lower-third rules may be relaxed in women and that ideal proportions differ across ethnic groups.[9]

The ratio is not tied to a single originator. It appears in looksmax.org threads where members ask for acceptable ranges, why it matters and how to fix a 'bad' ratio, and it travels together with other lower-third terms used in the community.[2][3][4][5][6] Wikipedia's coverage of looksmaxxing places the practice in online communities from the 2010s and its spread to TikTok in the early 2020s.[11] No source documents when the chin-to-philtrum ratio entered that vocabulary.

Threads ask for acceptable ranges and why the ratio matters.[4][5] In one, a poster with a short philtrum and a tall chin weighed a genioplasty to reduce vertical chin height against a combined upper-and-lower-jaw plan; a reply said a short philtrum with normal midface ratios would suggest bimaxillary surgery with chin height reduction, while adding that it was impossible to judge without photos.[2]

Another poster with a short philtrum asked about non-surgical options and was told a genioplasty could make the chin less tall and more forward-projected.[3] Other threads carry titles such as 'worst chin to philtrum ratio' and 'the ideal chin to philtrum ratio'.[6][7]
In the thread above, a reply cautions that it is impossible to judge the ratio without photos and other proportions.[2]

A lip lift shortens the skin between the nose and the upper lip so the upper lip sits higher and shows more vermilion. Wikipedia describes direct and indirect variants, including the subnasal 'bullhorn' lift, and notes that a 2014 systematic review found philtrum length decreased with indirect lip lifts.[12] A 2026 systematic review of 7 studies and 1,754 patients reported philtrum length falling from about 14.0 to 12.0 mm with a traditional bullhorn lift and from 14.5 to 10.75 mm with a Tri-Lift technique, mean Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale satisfaction of 4.4 out of 5, revision rates of 0.6 to 6.7 percent, and minor complications such as swelling, bruising, hypertrophic scarring, transient dysesthesia and asymmetry. The authors noted the studies were moderate at best in quality, with no randomised trials.[13]

Genioplasty is chin surgery that can use implants or bone movement; in a sliding genioplasty a segment of the jaw is cut and moved forward, backward or in height.[8] A 2025 narrative review describes vertical reduction (removal of surplus bone) and vertical augmentation, reports high aesthetic and functional success with stable long-term results, cites a 5.8 percent rate of temporary sensory loss in one series, and says careful tensioning of the chin muscle helps prevent lower-lip incompetence.[14] Common minor effects listed by Wikipedia include swelling, haematoma and temporary lower-lip numbness or weakness.[8]

Jaw surgery that moves the upper jaw, such as a Le Fort I osteotomy, belongs to orthognathic surgery, which Wikipedia describes as osteotomies on the upper jaw, lower jaw or both, with risks including bleeding, swelling, infection and nerve numbness that is usually temporary.[15] The looksmax.org thread above mentions a surgeon proposing 'downgrafting' of the maxilla to lengthen the midface and so rebalance the ratio, a plan the poster questioned.[2]

No studies found on the chin-to-philtrum ratio itself as a measure of attractiveness or surgical outcome. Related literature on lip and lower-face proportions, and on lip lift and genioplasty outcomes, is summarised above and is labelled as such.[9][10][13][14]

lore.intro: Forum threads treat the ratio as a quick diagnostic for the lower third and a prompt for surgery-planning questions, with members disagreeing about which direction of imbalance matters most.[2][3][4][5]

claims.claim: A short philtrum is ideal and should not be lengthened
A ratio near 1:2 (philtrum to chin) is the benchmark
Genioplasty can fix a tall chin relative to the philtrum
A lip lift can correct a long philtrum
Upper-jaw surgery can rebalance the ratio but may change the nose and philtrum
The ratio must be judged together with the whole face

timeline.event: Looksmaxxing communities form on forums such as the PSL sites, the setting in which facial ratios are discussed.[11]
A review of ideal lip proportions describes lower-third segments, including about 30% upper lip and 70% lip-plus-chin.[9]
A 3D photographic study of 100 Spanish adults reports reference measurements for lip, philtrum and chin dimensions.[10]
A narrative review of genioplasty describes vertical reduction and augmentation and reports stable results.[14]
A systematic review of lip lift techniques reports philtrum shortening, high satisfaction and low revision rates across 7 studies.[13]
